sets.title: The Last Evening at the Stall
paragraphs: The shutters of the Block 216 market were already half down when Jun arrived, but his grandfather’s stall glowed at the far end like the last lit window on a dark street. Ah Gong sat on his low stool exactly as he had for forty-one years, a shoe clamped between his knees, as if tomorrow were an ordinary day.

It was not. A notice taped to every pillar announced that the market would close for upgrading at midnight. The new plan had space for a café, a pharmacy and a bubble tea shop. It had no space for a man who mended soles and cut keys.

“You’re late,” Ah Gong said without looking up. “Pass me the small hammer.” Jun passed it. He had practised a speech on the bus — about how sorry he was, about how unfair it all was — but the words dissolved the moment he saw his grandfather’s hands. They moved the way they always had, quick and certain, tapping tiny nails into leather as though the shoe were the only thing in the world that mattered.

Customers came in a steady trickle all evening. None of them, Jun noticed, seemed to need anything urgently. A woman brought a single sandal with a strap that was barely loose. A taxi driver wanted a spare key cut for a flat he had sold years ago. An old man simply stood there holding a perfectly good umbrella until Ah Gong took it from him, opened it, closed it, and solemnly handed it back. “No charge,” he said. The old man nodded, eyes bright, and shuffled away.
“Why did he bring an umbrella that isn’t broken?” Jun whispered. Ah Gong threaded a needle. “He didn’t come for the umbrella.”

Jun looked down the emptying corridor and finally understood. They had been arriving all night with their flimsy excuses, these neighbours, because none of them knew how to say goodbye to a man who had never once asked for thanks. His throat tightened. For years he had been faintly embarrassed by the stall — its smell of glue, its hand-painted sign, the way his classmates’ parents worked in offices with glass doors. Now he wished he could go back and shake that younger self by the shoulders.

At ten to midnight, Ah Gong switched off the grinding machine. The silence it left behind was enormous. He unhooked the wooden signboard, wiped it with his sleeve and, to Jun’s surprise, held it out to him. “Too heavy for me,” he said, though it plainly was not.

Jun took the sign in both arms. It was lighter than he expected and heavier than anything he had ever carried. Together they pulled the shutter down, and the old man walked out of the market without once looking back. Jun looked back for both of them.

sets.title: What Is Standing Behind the Stall
paragraphs: At half past five in the morning the wet market was already louder than my school canteen at recess. Auntie Hui Min tied a rubber apron round my waist, so new and stiff that it stood away from my body like a board, and pointed at the trays of crushed ice. “Pomfret here, threadfin there, prawns in front where people can see them. And don’t smile so much. They’ll think you’re hiding something.”

I had volunteered for this. My mother had mentioned, in the careful voice she keeps for other people’s troubles, that Auntie’s helper had gone home to Ipoh and that Auntie was managing the stall alone with a bad wrist. I had pictured myself weighing fish and handing over change, quick and capable. I had not pictured the smell, which climbed into my hair within minutes, or the floor, slick as a skating rink, or the way the fish stared up at me from the ice with their flat silver eyes as if they already knew I was a fraud.

For the first hour I was mostly in the way. I gave a man change for a fifty when he had paid with a ten, and Auntie rescued the notes from his hand without a word. I wrapped a mackerel so badly that its tail poked out of the newspaper like a bookmark. Each time, Auntie only clicked her tongue and went on scaling, her knife rasping, her bandaged wrist held close to her body.

Then the woman with the jade bangle arrived, just as Auntie had gone to fetch more ice. The other customers seemed to make room for her without being asked. She did not look at me. She looked at the fish, one tray at a time, the way a teacher looks down a row of desks. “Where is Hui Min?” “Getting ice. I can help you, Auntie.” Her eyebrows rose a careful millimetre. “Then choose me a pomfret. A fresh one. For steaming.”

My mind emptied. Eight pomfret lay before me, identical as coins. I reached for the biggest, and saw the corner of her mouth move — not a smile, but the beginning of a verdict. So I stopped. What had Auntie said in the van, while I was half asleep? Eyes clear, not cloudy. Gills red, not brown. Press the flesh, and it should spring back. I put the big one down. I lifted the gill of the next fish with a finger that was not quite steady, then the next, and at the fourth I found a red as bright as fresh chilli. I pressed its side. It pushed back.

“This one,” I said. “The big one is from yesterday.” It was out before I thought about it — telling a customer that our own fish was old. My ears burned. The woman took the pomfret from me, lifted the gill herself, and pressed exactly where I had pressed. “Hm,” she said. She paid in exact change, counted into my palm coin by coin, and left.

When Auntie came back, dragging the sack of ice with her good hand, I confessed everything in one breath. I waited for the click of her tongue. Instead she laughed, a short bark that startled the prawn seller next door. “Madam Goh? Twenty years she has been coming here. She knows fish better than I do. She does not need anybody to choose for her.” “Then why did she ask me?” Auntie shrugged and tipped the ice over the trays. “To see what is standing behind my stall.”

By closing time my fingers were wrinkled and I smelled like the bottom of a fishing boat. Auntie hosed down the floor. Then she untied her own apron — soft, faded, moulded by years — and hung it on the nail beside mine. “Same time on Saturday,” she said. It was not a question, and I found I did not want it to be.

sets.title: In Case the Lift Moves
paragraphs: The lift stopped between the ninth and tenth floors with a jolt like a hiccup, and then the light went out. It did not dim. It went, as completely as a candle pinched between two fingers. Somewhere far below, a generator failed to start.

“Cool,” said Kiran. He was nine, and believed that anything which interrupted homework was an adventure. Arjun heard him bounce on his heels, heard the plastic bag of prata from the coffee shop swing against the wall. Arjun himself did not move. He was sixteen, a prefect, the boy who had been trusted to fetch dinner and his brother in one trip, and his heart was going like a fist on a door.

The dark in a lift is not like the dark in a bedroom. There is no grey square of window, no thread of light under a door. It pressed against his open eyes like a wet cloth. He found the wall with his palm and kept it there; the metal was cold and real. “Press the alarm,” Kiran said. “I’m pressing it.” He had been pressing it for some time. Nothing rang.

“Are you scared, Anna?” “Don’t be silly.” The words came out too fast and a little too high, and he coughed to cover them. “It’s a power failure. The whole block, probably. Someone will come.” He was grateful, at least, that the dark hid his face. For six years he had slept with the corridor light on, and had told his mother it was so that Kiran would not trip on the way to the toilet.

Minutes passed, or what felt like minutes; without light, time had no edges. Arjun counted his breaths the way the school counsellor had once taught the whole class before the examinations. In for four. Out for four. Beside him the bouncing had stopped. Then a small hand found his sleeve, travelled down it, and closed around two of his fingers.

“I’m not scared,” Kiran announced. “I just think we should hold hands. In case the lift moves suddenly.” “That’s sensible,” Arjun said. The hand was warm and slightly sticky with curry. He held it as carefully as he would have held a cup filled to the brim, and something in his chest that had been clenched since the light went out loosened by a notch. “Tell me about your football match,” he said. So Kiran did, at length, pass by pass, including the goal that was definitely not offside, and Arjun asked more questions than he had asked in a year.

They had reached the second half when the lights stuttered on. Both boys flinched. In the sudden white glare, the lift was only a lift: scratched steel, a notice about bulky items, two brothers and a bag of cooling prata. Kiran looked at their joined hands, then up at Arjun’s face, which was damp at the temples. Arjun waited for it — the crow of delight, the story that would be told at dinner tonight and at every dinner after.

Kiran let go and scratched his nose. “You were holding quite tight,” he said. “In case the lift moved,” said Arjun. “Ya. In case.” The doors slid open on the tenth floor. Kiran marched out first, swinging the bag, and stopped at their gate. “Anna,” he said, not turning round. “Tonight can we leave the corridor light on? I think I might trip.”

sets.title: Overdue
paragraphs: We found it while clearing Atok’s wardrobe, three weeks after the funeral: a hardcover book in a brown-paper jacket, tucked beneath his folded sarongs as if it were something precious or something shameful. Inside the cover was a paper pocket and a slip of stamped dates. The last stamp, in violet ink gone pale with age, said 14 MAR 1979.

“More than forty years overdue,” my mother said, and laughed, and then stopped laughing and had to sit down on the bed. The book was a guide to shore birds, with painted plates. Atok had put neat pencil ticks beside some of them — the kingfisher, the little heron, the sandpiper — and beside each tick a place and a date. The last tick was from only two years ago, in handwriting that shook.

“Take it back,” my mother told me. “He hated owing people.” I did not want to. I worked out the fine on my phone, at so many cents a day, and got a number that made my stomach drop. More than that, I did not want to hand the ticks to a stranger behind a counter. But my mother had the look of someone holding herself together with clothes pegs, so on Saturday I took the book on the bus, in a plastic bag on my lap, like a pot of something that might spill.

The library was nothing Atok would have recognised. Glass doors breathed open by themselves. Machines swallowed returned books through a slot and blinked green. I stood before one of them for a long time. The slot was the width of a letterbox and just as final. A small boy behind me sighed loudly, the way people do when they want you to know they are being patient.

I stepped out of the queue and went to the desk instead. The librarian was a tall man with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair. I had my explanation ready — my grandfather, the wardrobe, I can pay a bit every month — but it came out backwards and tangled, and in the end I simply slid the book across. He opened it at the date slip. He was quiet for so long that I began counting the ceiling lights.

“Nineteen seventy-nine,” he said at last, almost fondly. “This branch wasn’t even built. It would have come from the old place by the river, the one with the fans that never worked.” He turned the pages slowly and stopped at a tick. “Your grandfather saw a blue-eared kingfisher at the reservoir? I’ve been trying to see one for eleven years.” He did not sound like a man about to mention money.

“The fine—” I began. He tapped at his keyboard, frowned, tapped again. “This title was written off before I was hired. As far as our records are concerned, it doesn’t exist.” He closed the cover with two hands, the way you close a door on a sleeping child. “I can’t fine a book that doesn’t exist. I can’t put one on a shelf, either.” He pushed it back across the desk. “I think it had better stay lost.”

I carried the book home on my lap again, more carefully than before. That evening my mother found me at the window with it open, squinting at a brown bird on the railing of the opposite block. I had a pencil. It was an ordinary mynah, I am fairly sure, and it flew off before I could decide; but I had already turned to the back, where there was a clean page, and written the date.

sets.title: The Last Leg
paragraphs: The stadium smelled of rain on hot rubber. I stood in the fourth lane with my toes behind the line, shaking out my hands, and tried not to look at the patch of track ten metres ahead where, a year ago, the baton had bounced once, twice, and rolled under the feet of a girl from another school.

Nobody had blamed me. That was the worst part. Coach had said, “It happens,” and my teammates had hugged me in a damp, kind knot, and for weeks afterwards people in the corridor were so gentle with me that I felt like a cracked plate everyone had agreed not to mention. I would have preferred shouting. Shouting ends.

This year Coach had put me on the last leg again. When the list went up, I went to her office with a speech about Mei Xuan being faster out of the bend. She listened to all of it, capping and uncapping her pen. “Are you asking me or telling me?” she said. “Asking.” “Then no.” She went back to her marking. That was the whole conversation, and I carried it around for a month like a splinter in my thumb.

The gun cracked. From where I stood, the first two legs were a smear of colours on the far side, and the announcer’s voice was a kite with its string cut, drifting somewhere above the noise. Then Mei Xuan came off the bend in third place, her face twisted with effort, and the whole world narrowed to the yellow tube in her right hand.

All season we had drilled it: start running when she hits the tape mark, do not look back, reach behind, trust. In practice my hand had been steady. Now I felt it tremble behind me like a leaf in a drain. Three strides. Four. Every part of me wanted to turn my head — just a glance, just to be sure — and I knew with perfect clearness that a glance was exactly how I had dropped it the last time.

I kept my eyes on the lane. “HAND!” Mei Xuan screamed, and the baton slapped into my palm so hard that it stung, and my fingers shut on it like a trap. I do not remember deciding to run. The straight came up to meet me. I passed one girl on the outside, her breath loud and ragged at my shoulder and then gone. The leader was a red vest four metres ahead, then three, and then there was no more track.

Second. By less than an arm. I bent over with my hands on my knees and waited for the old feeling to arrive, the cracked-plate feeling. It did not come. My team crashed into me from behind, shrieking, and this time the hug was not careful at all; somebody’s elbow caught my ear.

Coach was the last to walk over. She did not say well done. She looked at the baton, which I had not noticed I was still gripping, my knuckles pale around it, and held out her hand. I had to think about how to open my fingers. “Same leg next year,” she said, and this time I knew better than to ask.

sets.title: Watch the Water
paragraphs: Mei Lin had been given one job for the school holidays, and it was standing beside her at the kerb, gripping the strap of a backpack that was still creased from the shop. Her cousin Jian had landed four days ago from a town in the hills where, as far as she could tell, nothing had ever moved faster than a goat. Now six lanes of traffic roared past them like a river in flood, and he was looking at it with an expression she could not read.

“It’s easy,” she said, in the bright, slow voice she used for the neighbour’s toddler. “Red man, we wait. Green man, we walk. The numbers tell you how many seconds are left.” She pointed. He nodded. He had nodded at everything since the airport — at the lift, at the escalator, at the rice cooker that sang when it finished — and said almost nothing, and she had decided privately that there was not very much going on behind the nod.

The green man appeared. Mei Lin stepped off the kerb. Jian did not. She was a third of the way across before she realised she was alone, and had to trot back with her face burning while a row of motorcyclists watched from behind their visors. “Green means go,” she hissed. “Did you not see it?” “I saw,” he said. He was not looking at the lights at all. He was looking to the right, where a delivery van was nosing round the corner and into the crossing as the last walkers scattered out of its way.

“He isn’t supposed to do that,” Mei Lin said. “No,” Jian agreed mildly. “But he did.” They waited through a whole cycle. She tapped her foot and thought of her friends at the mall, of her bubble tea sweating on a table without her. He stood with his weight on his toes, as still as a heron in a canal, and watched: not the green man but the wheels, the drivers’ heads, the gap between the bus and the car behind it.

When the light changed again he said, “Now,” a full second before she would have moved, and took hold of her sleeve — not her hand; her sleeve, lightly, between two fingers. She almost shook him off. She was fifteen; she had crossed this road a thousand times with her eyes on her phone. But his grip, light as it was, had a kind of practised certainty, and she let it stay. They crossed at his pace, which was quicker than hers. He let go the instant her shoe touched the far kerb.

“You’ve done this before,” she said. It came out like an accusation. He shrugged. “Not this.” And then, because she kept looking at him, he told her in his careful, textbook English about the river at the bottom of his town: how the bridge washed away each rainy season, how the schoolchildren crossed on the stones, how for three years it had been his task to take his small sister over, holding her by the sleeve because her hands were always full of books. “The water doesn’t follow rules,” he said. “So you watch the water. Not the sign that says the water is safe.”

Mei Lin opened her mouth and found that her toddler voice had gone. She thought of the nodding, and of what she had assumed lay behind it, and something uncomfortable turned over in her stomach. “Who takes her across now?” she asked. Jian looked back at the road, at the six lanes roaring behind them. For the first time she could read his face perfectly. “She’s eleven,” he said. “She says she is big enough.”

sets.title: The Short Cut
paragraphs: I should say at the start that the map was in my hands because I had taken it, not because anyone had given it to me. Mr Ong had held it out to the four of us at the jetty, and I had simply been the quickest. “Two kilometres to the campsite,” I announced, glancing at it for about as long as you glance at a bus number. “Follow me.”

I had been to the island once before, with my father, when I was seven. I remembered a quarry lake, a wild boar and an ice-cream. On the strength of this I considered myself a local. So when the gravel path curved left, the long way round a hill, and a narrow trail ran straight on into the trees, I did not hesitate. “Short cut,” I said. Farah, who was the smallest of us and had hardly spoken on the ferry, looked at the trail and then at the map in my fist. “Shouldn’t we check?” “I’ve checked,” I said, which was not true.

For twenty minutes the trail behaved itself. Then it began to thin, the way a stream thins in a drought, until it was only a suggestion between the ferns. The trees closed over us and the light turned green, as if we were walking along the bottom of a pond. Haziq stopped joking. Jun Wei, behind him, asked how much further it was, and I said, “Nearly there,” in the voice my father uses when he is driving and has missed the exit.

The truth arrived all at once, like cold water down the collar. We came to a fallen trunk furred with moss, with a hollow in it shaped like a mouth — and I had seen that mouth before. Half an hour before. We had walked in a circle, and I had led it. I unfolded the map properly for the first time. It was a tangle of brown lines that meant nothing to me, and I held it a little higher so that the others could not see my hands.

“We’re lost, right?” said Haziq. Nobody answered. Somewhere a cicada started up like a drill. It was five o’clock, and under the trees it was already later than that. I thought of saying that the map was wrong. I thought of saying it was a test and I had known all along. The lies queued up politely, one behind another, and what came out of my mouth, to my own surprise, was: “Yes. I’m sorry. I don’t know where we are.”

Saying it was like putting down a bag I had not known I was carrying. And it was Farah who picked it up. She did not say I told you so. She took a stub of pencil from her pocket and pointed with it — not at the map, but back the way we had come. “I’ve been snapping a twig at every fork,” she said, almost apologetically. “On the left side. In case.” She had not trusted me for one minute, I realised, and she had been too polite to say so.

We followed her twigs back, one after another, like beads on a string, and came out onto the gravel as the sky was going orange. At the campsite Mr Ong looked at his watch, then at our scratched legs. “Who was navigating?” I felt the others not look at me. It was a generous kind of not-looking, and I did not deserve it. “I was,” I said. “Badly. Farah got us back.”

Mr Ong only nodded and wrote something on his clipboard. That night, when the routes for the morning hike were given out, I took our map from the pile, carried it across the wet grass and put it into Farah’s hands. She unfolded it at once, the right way up, and began to read. I held the torch.

sets.title: Room Four
paragraphs: The waiting area outside Room Four smelled of floor polish and other people’s nerves. I sat with my scale book shut on my lap, because opening it now would only prove how much I had forgotten. Beside me, my mother was reading the same page of her magazine for the fourth time.
When the door opened, the boy before me came out with his ears red and walked straight past his father. “Next,” said a voice from inside. It was just a word, put down like a coin on a counter.

The examiner was a thin woman with grey hair cut as straight as a ruler’s edge. She did not smile or ask how I was. She looked at her form, then at the piano, and that was the whole of my welcome. “Scales,” she said. “B flat minor. Hands together.” My fingers had played that scale every morning since March, and now they felt as if they belonged to somebody else. I got through it the way one crosses a drain on a narrow plank — quickly, and without looking down.

Her pen scratched. It was the only sound in the room. I tried to read her face, but there was nothing on it to read. Mrs Devi, my teacher, nodded along when I played and hummed the tune under her breath; this woman sat as still as the metronome on the shelf with its arm locked.

The first two pieces passed in a blur. The third was the slow one, the one Mrs Devi said I always played “like someone reading out a shopping list”. Halfway down the second page, my left hand landed on a wrong chord. It was not a small slip; it sat in the air like a dropped plate. Every lesson I had ever had told me to keep going. Instead I stopped. My hands hovered. I heard myself say, “Sorry. May I start again from the top of the page?”
For the first time, the examiner looked up from her form. I waited for the sigh, or for the glance at the clock. “You may,” she said. That was all. But she put her pen down.

I do not know why that mattered so much. Perhaps it was because, for a moment, nobody was writing about me. I began again and, since the worst had already happened, there was nothing left to guard. I stopped counting. I let the slow notes take the time they wanted. Somewhere in the middle I forgot the woman at the desk altogether, and played it the way I played at home when the flat was empty, with the windows open and nobody listening — as if it were mine.
When the last note faded, the pen stayed where it was a second longer than it needed to. Then she picked it up and wrote something short. “Thank you,” she said. “Close the door gently, please.”

My mother stood up so fast that her magazine slid to the floor. “Well? What did she say?” “Almost nothing,” I said, and found, to my own surprise, that I was smiling. On the way to the bus stop she asked whether I thought I had passed. I told her honestly that I did not know. What I did not tell her was that I was no longer certain that was the question.

paragraphs: The alarm went off at ten to four, and for a moment Hafiz could not remember what he had agreed to. Then he heard the kettle, and his mother’s slippers on the kitchen floor, and he remembered. His father’s knee was in a brace until December. Somebody had to push the trolley.

Downstairs, the void deck was lit like an empty stage. A van had left the bundles beside the letterboxes, bound with plastic straps. His mother cut the straps with a small blade and began to count, her lips moving. Hafiz yawned so widely that his jaw clicked. “Block 412 first,” she said. “Top floor down. And don’t let the gate bang — people are sleeping.”

He had imagined it would be easy. Paper weighs nothing; everybody knows that. But eighty newspapers together weighed about as much as his little sister, and by the third block the strap of the bag had dug a groove into his shoulder. His mother, a head shorter than he was, moved along the corridors ahead of him like water finding its way downhill — never hurrying, never stopping. She folded each paper in one motion and slid it through the cold bars of the gate so that it landed flat, with hardly a whisper.

Hafiz’s first one hit a shoe rack and scattered across somebody’s doorstep. He looked up, expecting a scolding. His mother only knelt, gathered the pages, squared them against her knee and set them down properly. “The uncle at number 118 likes his on the stool, not the floor,” she said. “His back is bad.” “How do you know?” “Eleven years,” she said, and walked on.

Eleven years. He did the sum without wanting to. She had started when he was three. All those mornings he had come to the table at half past six and found her there with his breakfast, her hair neatly tied, asking whether he had packed his PE shirt — she had already done this. He had thought she simply woke up early. He had never once asked for what.

At a flat on the sixth floor, a light was on. An old woman in a faded blouse was waiting behind the gate, and she took the paper straight from his mother’s hand. “This is your boy? So tall.” She pushed two packets of soya milk through the bars. “Every Saturday she gives,” his mother said in the lift, as if it needed explaining. Hafiz held the packets against his chest. After hours of metal gates and damp newsprint, they were the first warm thing he had touched all morning.

By the last block the sky had gone from black to the colour of weak tea. Birds had started up in the rain trees. His legs trembled on the stairs and his fingers were grey with ink, but something else had changed too: his papers were landing flat. Not all of them. Most.

They sat on the kerb beside the empty trolley and drank the soya milk. His mother looked at her watch. “Six-oh-five. Faster than with your father,” she said, and then, because praise did not come naturally to her, “Don’t tell him.” “Same time tomorrow?” Hafiz said. He had meant it to sound like a complaint. It came out as something else, and she heard it, and looked away towards the brightening road so that he would not see her face.

sets.title: The Blue Rope
paragraphs: From the jetty, the sea at Kampung Teluk Batu had looked like a sheet of hammered tin, flat and harmless. Nadia had taken three photographs of it before breakfast. Now, an hour out in her uncle’s boat, with the village shrunk to a line of rust-coloured roofs, she understood that the sea was not something one looked at. It was something one was on, and it did not care whether she was comfortable.

Pak Long stood at the stern under the one patched sail, with a bare foot on the tiller, steering as casually as other people scratch an itch. He had said perhaps twenty words to her since she arrived from Singapore four days ago, most of them “Eat”. Her mother called him stubborn. Watching him haul in the first net hand over hand, Nadia thought the word was too small.

It was she who saw the cloud first, though she did not know what she was seeing. Far to the east the sky had turned the purple-grey of an old bruise, and under it the water had lost its shine. “Pak Long,” she said, “is that rain?” He glanced over his shoulder for no longer than a breath. Then he looked at the net still in the water, at the few fish already silver in the hold, and at her. She watched him weigh the three.
“We go back,” he said. He began pulling in the net, half empty, fast. He did not sound afraid, and that frightened her more than shouting would have.

The wind arrived before the rain did, and every wave it touched stood up white. The boat, which had rocked like a cradle all morning, began to buck. Spray hit Nadia’s face, warm and salty. Her phone was in her pocket; for once it did not occur to her to take it out. She gripped the wooden bench until her knuckles hurt, and stared at the back of her uncle’s faded shirt as if it were the only steady thing in the world.

“Nadia.” He had to say it twice. “The blue rope. Hold. When I say, you let go — not before.” He pointed with his chin. She crawled to it on her knees. The rope was wet and rough and alive, tugging like a dog that has seen a cat, and she wrapped it twice around her fist the way she had seen him do. She was shaking. She held on anyway.

The rain came down all at once, as though someone had slit a bag. She could no longer see the roofs. She could barely see her uncle. But she could hear him, and when at last he shouted “Now!” she opened her hand. Something heavy swung across above her head, and the boat, which had been fighting the waves, turned and began to run with them.

Twenty minutes later they bumped against the jetty. Her aunt was waiting under a sheet of plastic with a towel, scolding them both before the boat was even tied. Pak Long said nothing. He lifted the single basket of fish onto the planks, then reached down and pulled Nadia up after it with one hard, wet hand.

He did not let go at once. He turned her palm over. The rope had left two red stripes across it. He looked at them for a moment, nodded once, and went to see to his boat. Nadia closed her hand around the stripes, as carefully as if they were something she had been given.

sets.title: Dry or Soup
paragraphs: By my third week at the new school I had become very good at a certain blank look. I used it whenever my classmates dropped into Mandarin, which they did for jokes, for complaints about teachers and for anything else worth hearing. I would tilt my head, smile politely and wait, like a tourist who has wandered into the wrong queue.

It was a lie, of course. In the town across the Causeway where I had lived until June, Mandarin was what I had argued in, dreamed in and been scolded in. But on my first day here I had read a passage aloud in English, and a boy at the back had repeated my “three” — “tree” — just loudly enough. The laugh that followed was small. I carried it home anyway, like a stone in my shoe. That night I decided that if they were going to hear only one thing from me, it would be careful English, with every edge sanded off. When someone asked, I said my Chinese was “quite bad, actually”. After that it was easier to keep lying than to stop.

The noodle stall at the end of the canteen was run by a woman everyone called Auntie Lian. She had forearms like a baker’s and a ladle she used for pointing. On my first visit she asked me something rapid in Mandarin — dry or soup, I knew perfectly well — and I said, “Sorry, I don’t understand.” She looked at me for a second longer than was comfortable. Then she switched to English that was as short as mine was polished. “Dry. Soup. Which?”
After that I ordered with my finger. She served me without a word, but I felt her watching, the way you feel sun on the back of your neck.

The Thursday it happened, the queue was long and I was thinking about a Maths test. As she set my bowl on the counter, Auntie Lian said, quite softly and entirely in Mandarin, “Careful, I filled it to the top.” My hands, already reaching, slowed and took the bowl by its rim. I had done it before I knew I had done anything. Not a drop spilled.

I looked up. She was already ladling the next order, but one corner of her mouth had moved. I stood there with my ears burning, waiting for her to announce it to the whole queue. She did not. She said only, still in Mandarin and still not looking at me, “When I first came here from my village, I did not open my mouth for a year. People thought I was proud. I was only tired.” She tapped the ladle on the pot. “A shut mouth is heavier than this soup. Next!”

I should have walked away. Instead I heard my own voice thank her — in Mandarin, the first words of it I had spoken aloud at school in nineteen days. They came out rusty. She nodded as if I had merely paid.

I carried the bowl back to the table. Jia Le was in the middle of a story about his grandmother and a parking fine, and he had reached the part he could only tell in Mandarin. I knew the kind of sentence it was going to be. I felt the blank look rising to my face out of habit, the head already beginning its tilt. Then the ending came, and I laughed — too early, before anybody had translated a word.
Jia Le stopped. “I thought you couldn’t—” “I’m better at listening,” I said. It was not the whole truth yet. But it was nearer, and the soup, I noticed, had not gone cold.

sets.title: Thirty-One Cartons
paragraphs: By nine o’clock the flat had stopped looking like ours. Thirty-one cartons stood in the living room, each labelled in my mother’s square capitals, and the walls, stripped of their calendars and clocks, showed pale rectangles where our life had hung. The movers were coming at seven. My job was the storeroom, which nobody had properly opened since I was in primary school.

The first thing I found was not in the storeroom but on it: the height chart. It was not a real one, only the edge of the door frame, with pencil lines and dates in my father’s handwriting. It ended when I was twelve, the year I announced that I was too old for it. I ran my thumb up the marks. They climbed in great leaps near the bottom and crowded together near the top, like someone getting tired on a staircase. You cannot pack a door frame. I took a photograph, which is not the same thing.

Inside, I pulled out the rice cooker with the cracked lid, which my mother had refused to throw away for ten years “in case”. Then my brother’s football boots, stiff as dried fish, from the single season he had played. Then a biscuit tin. I knew that tin. It had sat on top of the fridge all through my childhood, and I had believed, for longer than I like to admit, that it held biscuits.

It held receipts, a spare key to a gate we no longer had, and every report book I had ever brought home, in order. I opened the Primary Four one. “Talkative. She can do better,” a teacher had written. Under it, in blue ballpoint, my mother had signed her name — and beside her signature, so small that I had to tilt the page, she had added a tick. Just a tick. It was there in every book. I had never noticed; I had only ever checked that she had signed, so that I could hand the book in.

“Ma,” I called, “why did you keep all these?” She came to the doorway wiping her hands, saw the tin and took it from me the way you take scissors from a child. “Rubbish,” she said. “I forgot they were there.” She put the tin in the carton marked KITCHEN — FRAGILE, between the good bowls, and taped it shut herself.

My father, meanwhile, had spent forty minutes failing to pack one clock. It was the ugly brown one from the hallway that had run seven minutes ahead for as long as I could remember; we had all simply learned to subtract. He kept wrapping it in newspaper, unwrapping it and holding it to his ear. “The new place has a clock on the oven,” my brother told him. “And on every phone.” “Those are correct,” my father said, as though that were a fault. He wound it, set it seven minutes fast and laid it on top of his own shirts.

Near midnight we ate instant noodles sitting on cartons, because the table was already in pieces. Nobody said anything large. My mother complained that the new kitchen had no window. My brother said the lift there was faster. Without its curtains the room echoed, and our voices came back to us slightly wrong, like a recording of a family.

Afterwards, when the others had gone to lie down on mattresses on the floor, I went back to the storeroom door. I found a pencil in a carton marked MISC. I stood against the frame with my heels together, the way I used to be told to, laid the pencil flat on my head and made a line — a hand’s width above the last one — and wrote the date. Whoever came next would paint over it. I knew that. I switched off the light.

sets.title: The Empty Half-Hour
paragraphs: Ask any teenager what they fear most on a long bus ride, and the honest answer is rarely missing their stop. It is a flat battery. We have become so used to filling every spare minute with a screen that an empty half-hour now feels less like rest and more like a small emergency.

This is a recent change. A generation ago, waiting was simply part of the day. People stared out of windows, counted lamp posts and let their thoughts wander wherever they pleased. Nobody called this a skill. Yet researchers who study attention are beginning to suspect that we gave up something valuable when we gave up being bored.

Consider what the mind does when nothing is demanded of it. Left alone, it starts to tidy up. It sorts through the day’s events and stores what is worth keeping, which is why a lesson often makes more sense after a quiet walk than after another hour of revision. It also begins to make unexpected connections between ideas, and many writers and inventors say their best ones arrived in the shower or on a slow train rather than at a desk. Boredom pushes us to plan as well: an unoccupied mind drifts towards the future, rehearsing conversations and setting goals. Perhaps most importantly, sitting through a dull moment teaches patience. A person who can tolerate ten minutes of nothing is better prepared for the many worthwhile tasks, from learning an instrument to finishing a long book, that are not exciting at every step.

There is a social benefit too. A bored child in a room with other bored children will eventually invent a game, and in doing so will practise negotiating, compromising and leading. A child handed a tablet learns none of these. Even adults notice more about the people around them, and are more likely to start a conversation, when their hands are empty.

None of this means throwing away our phones. It means making deliberate room for idleness. Young people can begin by leaving one short journey a day unfilled, with the phone zipped inside the bag rather than held in the hand. They can switch off the notifications that tug at their attention every few minutes. They can keep a notebook nearby, so that a wandering thought has somewhere to land. And they can take up a slow hobby — baking, sketching, fishing — in which waiting is part of the pleasure. Families can help by agreeing on one screen-free hour each evening, which works only if the adults obey it as well.
The first few attempts will feel uncomfortable, even itchy. That discomfort is not a sign that something is wrong. It is the feeling of a mind stretching after sitting still for too long.

sets.title: The Slow Pen
paragraphs: My grandmother’s shopping lists were works of art by accident. Written on the backs of old envelopes, in a slanting hand that leaned forward like a person walking into the wind, they said eggs, soap and thread, and somehow they also said her. When I type my own list into my phone, it says eggs, soap and thread, and nothing else at all.

It is easy to see why the pen is losing. Typing is faster, tidier and kinder to those of us whose handwriting resembles a spider that fell into ink and crawled home. A typed message can be corrected without a trace and sent across the island in a second. In many classrooms the keyboard has quietly taken the pen’s place, and few students miss it. Why keep a slow tool when a quick one is within reach?

The answer is that the slowness is the point. Because the hand cannot keep up with a teacher’s voice, a student writing notes by hand is forced to choose what matters and put it in fewer words. Someone typing can take down every sentence without thinking about any of them. Forming each letter also takes effort, and what costs effort tends to stay: most of us remember a word we have written out far longer than one we have tapped. A page of paper holds no notifications either, so the writer’s attention stays where the pen is. And a pen is free in a way a keyboard is not. An arrow here, a circle there, a small diagram in the margin: ideas can be joined up on the page as quickly as they join up in the head.

Handwriting does other work besides. It is personal: no two hands are alike, and a note in a friend’s own writing carries something of the friend. It shows care, since everyone knows that a handwritten card took time that a forwarded greeting did not. It lasts — a letter in a drawer can be read fifty years on without a charger or a password. And for many people, writing a worry down by hand at the end of a long day is calming, as though the trouble has been lifted out of the head and set down somewhere safe.

None of this requires giving up the keyboard. It requires keeping the pen in practice. A student can begin by taking notes by hand in at least one subject. A paper diary or journal, even three lines a night, keeps the habit alive. Birthday wishes and thank-you messages can be written on cards rather than sent as texts. And when a problem refuses to be solved on a screen, it is worth planning it on paper first, where a messy first attempt costs nothing and can be crossed out with some satisfaction.

Of course, there will be complaints. Handwriting makes the wrist ache; it cannot be searched; it is occasionally unreadable even to its owner. All true. But we do not stop walking because buses exist. We walk because some things — the neighbourhood, the weather, our own thoughts — can only be noticed at that speed.

I have kept one of my grandmother’s envelopes. The paper has yellowed and the thread was used up long ago, but the handwriting still leans forward, still in a hurry, still unmistakably hers. I look at it sometimes when my phone reminds me, in its neat and nameless letters, to buy eggs.

sets.title: While the City Sleeps
paragraphs: At six in the morning, the void deck below my flat is spotless. The bins are empty, the floor is still damp and smells faintly of soap, and the only sign that anyone has been there is a yellow board warning me not to slip. For years I assumed, as a small child assumes about the tooth fairy, that this simply happened.

It does not simply happen. I learnt this on the night I came home very late from a cousin’s wedding and found the estate wide awake. A man was hosing down the bin centre. Two women were working their way along the corridor of the opposite block, their mops moving in step like rowers. Out on the main road, a sweeping truck crept beside the pavement with its brushes whirring. I had lived there for fifteen years and had never once seen my own neighbourhood being cleaned.

There are good reasons why the work is done while the rest of us sleep. Roads are almost empty, so a truck can crawl along the kerb without holding up a line of buses. Markets, food centres and shopping streets cannot be scrubbed while customers are standing in them. The air is cooler, which matters a great deal to anyone doing heavy work outdoors. And rubbish left until morning would not wait politely: by daybreak it would smell, and it would invite every rat and cockroach in the district to breakfast.

But the arrangement has a price, and it is the cleaners who pay it. They must sleep by day, when the rest of the block is drilling walls, practising the piano and slamming doors, so their rest is broken. They miss family dinners and their children’s bedtimes. The work itself is hard on the body: bending, lifting and pushing for hours. It can be dangerous too, for on a dark road a passing driver may not see a worker until it is too late. And because nobody is awake to watch, the work is rarely thanked. It is a strange sort of job in which the better it is done, the less anyone remembers that it was done at all.

The rest of us cannot take over the night shift, but we can make it lighter. We can tie rubbish bags properly so that they do not split in a cleaner’s hands. We can stop treating the ground as a bin, since every dropped wrapper is something a person must bend down to pick up. And when we do meet a cleaner, at whatever hour, we can do the simplest thing of all, which is to greet them and say thank you.

None of this is charity. A city is a shared home, and in any home the person who clears up after everyone else deserves at least to be noticed. We are quick to complain when a bin overflows. We might be equally quick to notice the hundreds of mornings when it does not.

I still leave for school at six, and the floor of the void deck is still damp. But I no longer think of the tooth fairy. I think of two mops moving in step in the dark, and I walk around the wet patch rather than through it.

sets.title: The Wrong Notes
paragraphs: For the first three months, my violin sounded like a cat being asked to do its homework. My family were kind about it. My mother closed the kitchen door “to keep the heat in”; my brother discovered a sudden love of the public library. I did not blame them. I would have left too, if I had not been the one holding the bow.

Nobody warns you about this stage. On a screen, a musician walks on, lifts an instrument and pours out something beautiful, and it looks as natural as breathing. What we do not see are the years of scraping, squeaking and starting again that came first. So beginners, hearing the gap between the music in their heads and the noise in their hands, decide that they have no talent. The instrument goes back into its case, and there it stays.

That is a pity, because the frustration is not a sign that the learning has failed. It is the learning. An instrument teaches patience, for a difficult passage only comes right after it has been played slowly many, many times. It teaches a learner to break a big task into small ones, mastering a piece two bars at a time rather than all at once. It trains careful listening, since nobody can correct a wrong note without first hearing it. And it makes progress something a person can actually hear: the tune that was impossible in March is merely hard in June, which is proof that effort works.

The rewards reach beyond the practice room. A student who has learnt to keep going at the piano is less easily defeated by a page of algebra. Playing in a band or an orchestra teaches a person to fit in with others — to wait, to keep time, to be one part of something larger. Performing, even for three aunts in a living room, builds the nerve to stand up in front of people. Then there is the simple matter of comfort: after a bad day, twenty minutes with an instrument can settle the mind in a way that scrolling never does. And unlike most things we learn at fifteen, it can stay with us for life.

How, then, does a beginner survive the early months? Practise a little every day rather than a great deal once a week. Choose at least one piece you actually like, alongside the ones your teacher sets. And record yourself now and then, so that on a discouraging evening you can play back last month and hear how far you have come.

sets.title: The Habit of the Bench
paragraphs: The bus stop outside my school is forty steps from the gate. The bus takes me two stops, a distance I could cover on foot in twelve minutes, and on most afternoons I wait nine minutes for it to arrive. I have done this sum many times, usually while waiting, and it has never once got me off the bench.

I am not alone on that bench. We have grown used to treating every journey as a problem to be solved in the fewest possible minutes. The phone in my pocket will happily plan the quickest route to anywhere, and it has never once suggested the pleasant one. Walking, in this way of thinking, is what happens when something has gone wrong: the bus is full, the rain has stopped the trains, or the fare card has run out of value.

Yet a short walk gives a good deal in return for its minutes. It is exercise that needs no special shoes, no fee and no appointment. After a day folded into a classroom chair, it loosens the body and clears a head stuffed with formulas. It gives the mind room to wander, and it is surprising how often a problem that would not move at a desk comes loose somewhere between two traffic lights. It is also dependable: a walk is never stuck in a jam and never sails past the stop because it is full.

The benefits do not end with the walker. On foot, you notice your own neighbourhood — which shop has changed hands, which tree is in flower, which uncle feeds the same cat every evening. You meet people instead of passing them behind glass, and a nod repeated every day slowly turns a stranger into a neighbour. Every short trip made on foot also frees a seat on a crowded bus for someone who needs it more. It adds nothing to the fumes that hang over the road. It even saves the fare, which is no small matter to anyone living on pocket money.

Nobody needs to give up wheels altogether. Begin by getting off one stop early and walking the rest of the way. Keep an umbrella and a pair of comfortable shoes ready, so that weather and blisters are no excuse. And walk with a friend when you can, since conversation shortens any road.

I admit the obvious objection. This is a hot, wet island, and there are afternoons when the air feels like soup and arriving anywhere dry is a victory. On those days, take the bus with my blessing. But be honest about the other days — the breezy ones, the after-rain ones — when the only thing stopping us is the habit of the bench.

Last week I finally did the sum with my feet. I walked past the bus stop, past the nine minutes of waiting, past a bakery I had not known existed, and reached my block just as the bus I would have taken pulled up beside me. We had arrived together. Only one of us had bought a curry puff on the way.

sets.title: More Than a Meal
paragraphs: Nobody goes to a hawker centre for the furniture. The stools are bolted to the floor, the tables wobble, and the ceiling fans push warm air from one side of the hall to the other. And yet, if you asked the people of my estate which building they could least bear to lose, I suspect the shopping mall would not even come second.

The food is the obvious reason, and it is a good one. A plate of chicken rice that costs less than a cup of coffee in the mall is not a small thing. But food can be delivered to the door these days in a paper bag. If eating were all a hawker centre was for, it would have emptied long ago. It has not, because people come for a good deal that is not written on any menu.

To begin with, it is one of the few places where everybody sits together. The taxi driver, the office manager and the student in PE shorts share one long table, and nobody finds it odd. It is also a daily meeting place for the old: the same retirees gather at the same table each morning, and for some of them that cup of coffee is the main conversation of the day. And it makes neighbours of strangers, because a stallholder who has seen you every week since you were in primary school knows your order by heart and notices when you look tired.

It teaches without meaning to. A child sent to buy four packets of noodles learns to queue, to speak up, to count the change and to carry the lot back without spilling. In the mixture of stalls — Malay, Chinese, Indian and everything in between — the young taste one another’s food long before they study one another’s festivals. The centre also keeps old recipes alive, dishes that take hours to prepare and that few of us would attempt at home. And it gives small cooks a living. A stall needs far less money to open than a restaurant, so a good recipe and hard work are nearly enough.

Places like this last only if they are used and looked after. We can eat there instead of ordering in, at least some of the time. We can try the quiet stall at the end of the row as well as the famous one with the queue. We can return our trays and leave the table fit for the next family. We can be patient at peak hours, remembering that the person behind the counter has been standing since before dawn. And the young can learn at least one of those old dishes from someone who knows it, before the knowledge retires with its owner.

I know the complaints. It is hot, it is noisy, the floor is sometimes wet, and a seat at noon must be hunted like treasure. A mall food court solves all of these with air-conditioning and matching chairs. But notice that nobody there knows your name, and nobody stays after the last mouthful. Comfort, it turns out, is not the same thing as belonging.

Last Sunday I watched an old man at the next table push his plate aside, take out a chess board and set up the pieces. Within minutes, another man had sat down opposite him without a word. The table still wobbled. Neither of them seemed to mind.

sets.title: Once Upon a Fact
paragraphs: I can tell you, in order, everything that happened to a mousedeer who tricked a row of crocodiles into forming a bridge. I heard the tale once, at the age of six, from an aunt who did all the voices. I cannot tell you a single date from the history chapter I revised last Thursday. Something is clearly unfair here, and I do not think it is my memory.

Teachers have always known this, even when timetables forget it. Tell a class that honesty matters, and thirty heads nod politely and remember nothing. Tell them about the boy who shouted about a wolf once too often, and they will carry it into old age. The lesson is identical. The packaging is not, and the mind, it seems, is fussy about packaging.

Why should a story stay when a fact slips away? One reason is that a story has an order. Each event causes the next, so remembering one part pulls the following part up after it, like links in a chain. A list of facts has no such chain; lose one, and nothing tugs it back. A story also makes pictures. We see the crocodiles lined up across the river, and what the mind has seen it keeps more readily than what it has merely been told. Then there is feeling: we worry for the mousedeer, we laugh when the trick works, and whatever moves us tends to be stored with care. A story is about someone, too, and we are naturally more interested in a character who wants something than in a number that wants nothing.

Stories also keep us guessing. We want to know what happens next, and that curiosity holds our attention in a way a fact rarely manages. They get passed on as well: a good story is retold at dinner, and every retelling presses it a little deeper. Finally, a story hands us the meaning along with the information. It does not simply report that pride is dangerous. It shows the proud character falling, so we understand why the fact matters.

None of this is an excuse to stop learning facts. It is a hint about how to learn them. sets.title: What the Queue Knows
paragraphs: If you want to understand a country, skip the museums and go and stand in a queue. At half past twelve outside a popular chicken rice stall, a line of hungry strangers, shuffling forward like one long and patient animal, will tell you more about how people here treat one another than any guidebook.

A queue is a stranger invention than it looks. Nobody is paid to guard it, and no rule is pinned to the wall. Yet twenty people who have never met arrange themselves in order of arrival and stay that way. It is an agreement made without a word and renewed every minute, and it is fragile: it lasts only as long as each person in it chooses to keep it.

Consider what an orderly queue reveals about the people in it. First, they accept that everyone is equal: the man with the expensive watch waits behind the schoolboy in slippers, because all that counts is who came first. They also trust strangers, since nobody would wait calmly unless they believed the people behind would not push past. A queue shows patience too, for each person in it has agreed to put off what they want now for the sake of order. It shows that people will keep a rule when no one is watching, without a policeman or a fine in sight. And when a line parts to let an old woman with a walking stick go ahead, it shows that fairness here has room for kindness.

None of this happens by itself; a queue is kept alive by small acts. The first is to join at the back, however late you are running. The second is not to hold places for others: one student guarding a spot is harmless until five classmates arrive to claim it. Be ready when your turn comes, with your order decided and your money in your hand, because those behind you pay for every second you spend dithering. Keep up as the line moves, too, rather than leaving a widening gap while you stare at your phone. If you cannot tell where a line ends, ask instead of guessing in your own favour. And when someone does cut in, say so politely; glaring at the back of a head has never moved anyone.

Queues can make fools of us as well. Open a new bubble tea shop, and a line will form simply because a line has formed. People at the back often have no idea what is being sold at the front; they assume that anything so many others are waiting for must be worth having. Here the queue is no longer a way of sharing fairly. It is an advertisement that the customers kindly stand in themselves.

Watch, though, what happens when the agreement breaks. A man slips in near the front, and for a moment nobody says anything. The cutting in is one person’s small theft. The silence is worse, because it tells everyone watching that the rule has no defenders. Within minutes the line begins to bunch and fray, elbows come out, and twenty polite people become a crowd.

So the next time you find yourself in line with a tray in your hands, look along it. You are standing in something people built without tools, a small country in single file. And if the auntie in front of you turns round and says, ‘You go first, you only have one drink,’ you will know what kind of country it is.

sets.title: The Last Free Room
paragraphs: There are not many places left where you can sit for four hours in air-conditioned comfort and spend nothing at all. The neighbourhood library is one of them. You may walk in with a full schoolbag or with empty hands, and nobody at the door asks why you have come.

It was not supposed to last. When every book could be squeezed into a phone, people said that libraries would soon go the way of the video rental shop. Why keep a whole building full of paper when the same words weigh nothing in your pocket? It was a reasonable prediction, and it was wrong, because it supposed that a library was only a warehouse for books. Spend a weekday afternoon in one and you will see how much else goes on there.

Start with the students. A flat shared with two younger brothers and a television is no place to revise, and the library offers what such a home cannot: a quiet desk. It offers books without a price, so that a child whose family buys few can still read a new one every week. It also lets readers try a subject they know nothing about, since a book on astronomy that is given up after ten pages has cost them nothing.

Then look at who else is there. The old men turning the pages of the newspapers by the window have come as much for company as for news; a morning among other people is better than a morning alone in a flat. At the computers, someone without internet at home is filling in a job application. And behind the counter sits a person whose whole job is to help you find information you can trust, which matters more, not less, now that anybody can publish anything.

A place this useful is kept so by the people who use it, and the rules are not difficult. Keep your voice down, and take your phone calls outside. Bring books back on time, because somebody else is waiting for the one on your bedside table. Treat them gently: a folded corner or a curry stain is a message to every later reader that you did not care. Do not leave a bag on a chair for half the day to hold a seat you are not sitting in. Put a book back where you found it, or on the trolley, for a book on the wrong shelf is as good as lost. Above all, borrow. A library that nobody uses is the easiest thing in the world to close.

What I like best, though, is what a library refuses to do. It does not hurry you. It does not play music to make you spend, or move you along with a queue number, or mind whether you look like someone who belongs. A boy in a school uniform and a retired taxi driver are given exactly the same chair. In a city where almost every square metre is trying to sell you something, that is rarer than it sounds.

Tonight, somewhere, a girl will finish her homework at a table she does not own, under a light she does not pay for, across from an old man asleep over the sports pages. Neither of them will think of it as a gift. That is the quiet part. The library is the neighbour who lends you the ladder and never mentions it.

sets.title: The Useful Flop
paragraphs: The best thing that happened to me in my first year of secondary school was a science project that fell apart in front of the whole class. It was a bridge made of ice-cream sticks, meant to carry five textbooks, and I had been so sure of it that I had not tried it once at home. It carried exactly one before folding up like a deckchair, and thirty-nine people laughed.

At the time I wanted the floor to open and swallow me. Yet nobody remembers that bridge now except me, and I remember it fondly. It cost me a few marks that no one has asked about since, and it taught me to test a thing in private before showing it off in public. That is the bargain of failing early: the price is small and the lesson is large. Make the same mistake ten years later, with real money and other people depending on you, and the lesson is no bigger, but the bill certainly is.

What does an early failure give you? To begin with, it shows you exactly what you do not know: a test you pass tells you little, but a test you fail points straight at the gap. It also takes away some of the fear of failing, because you discover that the sky stays where it was and that by Friday everyone has forgotten. And you get practice at picking yourself up and starting again, which is a skill like any other and is best learnt young.

There are quieter gains too. Nothing punctures a big head like a public flop, and a person who has been humbled is readier to listen to advice. Having stood there red-faced yourself, you become kinder to the next person it happens to. And failing tells you what you truly care about: if you still want another go after falling flat, the thing matters to you; if all you feel is relief, perhaps it never did.

Failing well, however, takes some method. Try difficult things first where little is at stake, in a class quiz or a friendly match and not in the final. When it goes wrong, admit that it did and that the fault was yours, without blaming the referee or the weather. Work out what went wrong while the memory is still fresh. Ask someone better than you what they noticed, since they will have seen what you could not. Then change one thing and try again soon, before the failure has time to harden into a reason for never trying.

I am not saying that failure is pleasant, or that it is good in itself; a failure you learn nothing from is merely a bad day. Nor are adults always a help. The parent who rushes a forgotten PE shirt to the school gate is delivering more than a shirt. That parent is taking away a cheap lesson and saving up an expensive one.

The ice-cream sticks went into the bin that same afternoon, and I was glad to see them go. I did not know then that I would be carrying them around for years. Every bridge I have built since, real or otherwise, has stood on the one that fell.

sets.title: The Drawer of Broken Things
paragraphs: Every home has a drawer where broken things go to wait. Ours holds three chargers, a torch, a pair of spectacles with one arm, and a radio that my grandfather insists he will fix one day. Nothing in that drawer has ever been fixed. It is less a workshop than a waiting room for the rubbish chute.

My grandfather, to be fair, grew up when mending was ordinary. A shoe went to the cobbler, a shirt got a new button, and a fan that stopped turning was opened up on the kitchen table. You bought a thing expecting to keep it. Today’s things are sealed shut with glue, and a new kettle costs less than an hour of a repairman’s time. So we replace, almost without thinking, and tell ourselves that it is only sensible.

Sometimes it is. But a thing we have repaired is not the same as a thing we have replaced, and the difference is worth noticing. To mend something you must first open it, so you end up understanding how it works. It gathers a history: the schoolbag with the restitched strap is the one that went to every camp, and no new bag can say that. Having spent an evening on it, you handle it more carefully afterwards. There is pride in it too, the plain satisfaction of having made a dead thing go with your own hands. Over the years it saves money, since a tube of glue is cheaper than a pair of shoes. And it keeps one more object out of the bin.

Repairing more is mostly a matter of small habits. Before you buy, check whether the thing can be opened and whether spare parts are sold for it. Learn a few simple skills, such as sewing on a button or gluing a sole. Keep a basic kit at home — needle, thread, glue, a screwdriver — because a repair that needs a trip to the shop rarely happens. Ask the older people in your family to show you how; they are usually delighted to be asked. When something breaks, give it a deadline instead of a drawer: try to fix it by the weekend. And what you cannot mend yourself, take to someone who can, like the cobbler under the block or the alteration shop at the market.

I do not want to make a religion of this. A phone battery that has begun to swell is dangerous, and should go. So should the cheap umbrella whose repair would cost three times what it is worth. Knowing when to let go is part of the craft.

What worries me is the habit, not the kettle. A person who throws things out at the first fault may come to believe that anything flawed is finished. It is a short step from there to dropping a hobby after one bad week, or a friend after one quarrel.

Last month I took the radio out of the drawer myself. It cost me two evenings, one borrowed screwdriver and a burnt thumb, and it now plays with a faint crackle, like an old man clearing his throat. It is the worst radio in the house. It is also the only one I would save from a fire.

sets.title: The Bell That Rings Too Early
paragraphs: At a quarter past six on a school morning, the least truthful sentence in the language is spoken in bedrooms all over the island: ‘I’m up.’ The speaker is not up. The speaker is lying flat with both eyes shut, bargaining with an alarm clock for five more minutes like a shopper haggling over the last fish at the market.

Adults have a ready explanation, and it is either laziness or the phone. There is some truth in the second. But anyone who can remember being fifteen knows that something odder is going on. A teenager seems to run on a later clock than the rest of the household. At eleven at night, when the parents are yawning, the fifteen-year-old is wide awake and full of plans; at seven the next morning, the same person can hardly spell their own name. The school timetable, however, was drawn up by people who wake easily at dawn. So the young are asked to do their hardest thinking at the very hour when they are least fit for it.

The cost of too little sleep is familiar to anyone who has sat in a classroom. The first lesson passes in a fog, because a tired mind cannot hold its attention on anything for long. What was revised the night before has slipped away by morning, as if it had been written on water. Tempers shorten, so that a harmless remark from a sister at breakfast starts a quarrel. Tired students make careless slips as well, misreading the question or missing the step off the bus. They seem to catch every cold that is going round. And they lose their appetite for the things they used to love: the keen footballer is suddenly too weary for training.

Some of the remedy lies with teenagers themselves. They can keep to the same bedtime every night, weekends included, since a body that never knows when to expect sleep will not offer it on demand. They can leave the phone to charge outside the bedroom. They can start their homework soon after dinner instead of at ten o’clock. And they can stay away from coffee and sweet bubble tea once evening comes.

The rest lies with adults. Parents can dim the lights and turn the television down late in the evening, for nobody falls asleep easily in a flat that is still wide awake. Schools can move the most demanding lessons away from the first period of the day. Neither change costs anything except the admission that the young are not simply being difficult.

None of this is an excuse. The boy who is still gaming at two in the morning cannot blame the timetable. But listen to how we talk about sleep. We praise the student who ‘burned the midnight oil’ and tease the one who was in bed by ten. We have made tiredness into a medal, and then we wonder why the young are so eager to wear it.

A timetable is only paper, and paper can be rewritten. A fifteen-year-old cannot. Until somebody moves the bell, the least we can do is stop calling them lazy, and let ‘I’m up’ be true a little more often.
